title: Quantum turbulence in the many-body regime
authors: Sayak Bhattacharjee, Mahendra K. Verma, Alexander V. Balatsky, Srinivas Raghu
abstract: We discuss phenomenology associated with turbulent hydrodynamics in quantum fluids from a condensed-matter perspective. We begin with weakly-interacting superfluids, often modeled by a mean-field theory governed by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation. Considering the effect of quantum fluctuations beyond the mean-field approximation, we propose a study of many-body quantum effects in turbulent hydrodynamics, especially near zero temperature. We motivate examples of quantum many-body systems where such effects may be uncovered. These include bosons confined in a periodic potential in low spatial dimensions (one and two), and the associated quantum critical point of the superfluid-insulator transition, realized in present-day ultracold-atom and quantum computing platforms. We conclude by listing a set of (open) questions that may be answered using modern quantum many-body techniques. This article is part of the theme issue 'Frontiers of turbulence and statistical physics'.
summary: This paper reviews the complex field of quantum turbulence, focusing on where mean-field theories fail due to strong quantum fluctuations. It synthesizes knowledge from superfluids and lattice models to argue that a complete description requires advanced many-body techniques beyond simple Gross-Pitaevskii approximations. The work highlights open questions regarding universal scaling laws in these non-equilibrium quantum regimes.
main_problem: The paper addresses the theoretical challenge of understanding turbulent hydrodynamics in quantum many-body systems when strong quantum fluctuations are present, moving beyond mean-field descriptions.
main_result: It establishes that while mean-field theories (like GP) capture classical inertial ranges, a full description requires accounting for strong quantum fluctuations, especially near critical points or at low dimensions.
method: The analysis synthesizes knowledge from continuum hydrodynamics (Euler/GP equations), lattice models (Bose-Hubbard), and field theory approaches to identify regimes where approximations break down.
model_or_system: The primary systems are superfluids, modeled using the Gross-Pitaevskii equation for mean-field analysis, but requiring extensions to second quantization or lattice Hamiltonians when fluctuations dominate. Specific examples include bosons in periodic potentials and low-dimensional condensates.
key_observables: Energy spectrum scaling ($\sim k^{-5/3}$), quantized circulation, density fluctuation magnitude ($\delta n / \langle nangle$), and the existence of multiple inertial ranges.
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), inter-vortex spacing ($\lambda$), healing length ($\xi$), and the ratio of quantum fluctuations to mean density ($\delta n / \langle nangle$).
main_assumptions: The paper contrasts regimes: near equilibrium (classical/mean-field) versus far from equilibrium where strong quantum fluctuations necessitate going beyond standard approximations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the energy cascade in classical vs. quantum turbulence, showing expected spectral deviations and phase diagrams for Bose-Hubbard models separating superfluid and Mott insulator phases.
paper_structure: The discussion progresses from reviewing mean-field descriptions (GP equation) to identifying limitations when fluctuations are strong, then detailing lattice models (Bose-Hubbard), and finally outlining the necessity of quantum kinetic theory for a complete picture.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it bridges classical turbulence phenomenology with modern many-body physics, suggesting new theoretical frameworks needed to describe non-equilibrium dynamics in ultracold atomic systems.
